name: Spironolactone
lead: Spironolactone (brand name Aldactone, among others) is a prescription steroidal medication that blocks aldosterone at the mineralocorticoid receptor and, to a lesser degree, blocks androgen receptors [1][2]. For appearance, the second action is the relevant one: androgens drive oil (sebum) production, acne, unwanted facial and body hair and pattern hair thinning, and by dampening androgen signalling in the skin and hair follicle the drug is used off-label to calm persistent acne, reduce oiliness, slow hirsutism and support hair density in women [1][4][11][14].

Its labelled uses are cardiovascular and renal: heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, add-on treatment of hypertension, and oedema in cirrhosis and nephrotic syndrome, with other approved uses including primary hyperaldosteronism and low potassium [1][3]. Dermatology use grew out of those prescriptions. A 2012 review says the antiandrogen effect was noticed in women treated for hypertension who also had polycystic ovary syndrome, and a systematic review notes off-label acne use since the 1980s [14].

The 2024 American Academy of Dermatology acne guideline makes a conditional recommendation for spironolactone, and two randomised trials, the SAFA trial in England and Wales and the FASCE trial in France, have tested it in adult women with acne [4][5][6]. The drug is also widely used as an antiandrogen in feminising hormone therapy [1], and it features in social media: a 2025 analysis of the 50 most-viewed TikTok videos on it found more than 100 million views in total [23].

Prescribing information warns of hyperkalaemia and recommends potassium monitoring, notes that it can cause gynecomastia, and reports feminisation of male fetuses in rat studies [3]. Because of these antiandrogen effects it is generally not used for acne or hair loss in men [1]. Wikipedia notes it was discovered in 1957 and introduced in 1959 [1].

paras: Wikipedia describes androgens as central to oily skin, acne, hirsutism and male pattern hair loss, and notes that spironolactone's antiandrogen activity is mainly responsible for its use in androgen-dependent skin and hair conditions in women, including acne, seborrhea, hirsutism, pattern hair loss and hyperandrogenism [1]. It is used for acne in women and sometimes combined with a contraceptive pill, with benefit potentially taking up to about three months to appear [1].

Acne. A 2012 review in the Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology describes spironolactone as a standard option for women with late-onset or persistent acne, cyclical flares or hormonal-pattern lesions, including those who have failed other treatments or cannot take isotretinoin. It reports improvement often within about 4 to 8 weeks and fuller response over roughly three months [14]. The 2024 AAD guideline lists it among its conditional recommendations, alongside combined oral contraceptives, minocycline and sarecycline [4].
Hirsutism and oily skin. It is described as a first-line treatment for hirsutism and has been compared with finasteride, flutamide and cyproterone acetate in that setting [1].

Hair loss. A 2023 systematic review of oral and topical spironolactone for androgenetic alopecia identified seven clinical studies (two randomised) covering 618 patients, 553 of them women. In four oral studies in women, 81 percent of participants showed hair-growth improvement on photographic or scoring assessment, and six studies combining spironolactone with other treatments, mainly minoxidil, reported better results than monotherapy in three comparisons. The authors note the evidence base is small and heterogeneous and call for larger randomised trials [11]. A broader 2024 review of hair-loss treatments lists many options and highlights the value of a multifaceted, individualised approach [12].

Men. Because of its antiandrogen effects, spironolactone is generally not used orally for acne or hair loss in men, according to prescribing overviews [1][14]. The NHS notes breast pain and enlargement can occur in men [24]. Topical spironolactone has attracted interest because little or no systemic absorption has been observed, according to Wikipedia, and the 2023 review found improvement in two small topical studies (a 1 percent gel randomised trial and a 5 percent solution study), with contact dermatitis in 20 percent of participants in one study; it found no study directly comparing topical with oral use [1][11].

Gender-affirming care. It is widely used as an antiandrogen in feminising hormone therapy, a use first studied in 1986, and it contributes to breast development and reduced body hair and oiliness in that context [1].

The US label lists heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (NYHA class III to IV), add-on therapy for hypertension, oedema in cirrhosis and nephrotic syndrome, and primary hyperaldosteronism among its indications [3]. The 1999 RALES trial in 1,663 people with severe heart failure was stopped early after a 30 percent relative reduction in death with spironolactone versus placebo [7]. In heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, the TOPCAT trial found no significant reduction in its primary composite outcome (18.6 percent versus 20.4 percent) [8]. In resistant hypertension the PATHWAY-2 crossover trial found spironolactone superior to placebo, bisoprolol and doxazosin as add-on therapy [9], and a 2025 JAMA trial compared it with amiloride [10].

Acne. In the SAFA trial, 410 women aged 18 or older with facial acne warranting oral antibiotics were randomised to spironolactone (201) or placebo (209) for 24 weeks. On the Acne-QoL symptom score (0 to 30, higher is better), the adjusted difference was 1.27 points at week 12 and 3.45 points at week 24 in favour of spironolactone. Self-assessed improvement at week 24 was 82 percent versus 63 percent, and investigator-rated treatment success at week 12 was 19 percent versus 6 percent [5].

In the French FASCE trial, 133 women with moderate adult female acne received either doxycycline plus benzoyl peroxide or spironolactone plus benzoyl peroxide. Spironolactone showed significantly greater treatment success at month 6 (p = 0.007), and the authors reported that quality of life was better with spironolactone and that it was well tolerated [6].

A retrospective review of 110 women treated at the University of Pennsylvania found that 85 percent showed some improvement and 55 percent reached a score of 0 at all sites, with average acne-score reductions of 73 percent on the face, 76 percent on the chest and 78 percent on the back. The study had no control group [13]. The 2012 review rates the evidence base from small trials as modest while describing spironolactone as a well-recognised option for adult women [14].

Onset and course. The 2012 review reports improvement often within about 4 to 8 weeks, fuller response around three months, and that benefit may level off after about a year; the SAFA authors observed larger effects at 24 weeks than at 12 [5][14].

The SAFA trial was a pragmatic, multicentre, phase 3, double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial of spironolactone in women with acne vulgaris in England and Wales, published in the BMJ in 2023. Headaches were more frequent with spironolactone (20 percent versus 12 percent) and no serious adverse reactions were reported [5]. The FASCE study, a multicentre randomised double-blind trial in France, compared spironolactone with doxycycline in moderate acne in adult women and was published in 2024 [6]. A 2012 practical review earlier summarised the observational data for post-teenage women [14].

The 2024 AAD guideline places spironolactone in its conditional recommendations, alongside combined oral contraceptives, sarecycline and minocycline [4]. A 2025 review of acne innovations discusses opportunities to improve patient experience with spironolactone [15], and a 2026 editorial in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology discusses the drug's role in acne [16].
For hair loss, evidence comes mainly from small studies summarised in a systematic review of oral and topical use [11]. A registered trial of spironolactone for melasma was withdrawn [17].
In the cardiovascular field, RALES, TOPCAT, PATHWAY-2 and a 2025 comparison with amiloride in resistant hypertension are the main randomised trials [7][8][9][10].

The label lists hyperkalaemia, hypotension and worsening renal function, electrolyte and metabolic abnormalities, and gynecomastia as clinically significant adverse reactions, and advises monitoring of potassium within a week of starting and periodically afterwards. Risk of hyperkalaemia rises with renal impairment, potassium supplements or potassium-containing salt substitutes [3]. In RALES, about 9 percent of male heart-failure patients developed gynecomastia, which is dose-dependent and usually reversible [3].

Skin and hair users. In the 110-woman retrospective review, 46 percent reported side effects and 5 percent stopped the drug; the most common were breakthrough bleeding or spotting, absent periods and lightheadedness [13]. The 2012 review lists menstrual irregularity, breast tenderness, lightheadedness and increased urination, notes that combining spironolactone with a combined oral contraceptive can reduce menstrual and breast effects, and says hyperkalaemia is uncommon in healthy young women but of greater concern with kidney or heart disease, potassium supplements or certain other drugs [14]. In the 2023 alopecia review, oral side effects were menstrual disorders (7.9 percent), dizziness or headache (6.5 percent), facial hypertrichosis (4.1 percent), rash (2.3 percent) and hyperkalaemia (0.9 percent) [11]. The NHS lists dizziness, nausea, cramps, tiredness and breast pain or enlargement as common and rare allergic, liver, kidney and skin reactions as serious [24].

Interactions and contraindications. The label contraindicates use with hyperkalaemia, Addison's disease or eplerenone; the NHS notes interactions with digoxin, potassium supplements and NSAIDs such as ibuprofen [3][24]. A population study found hospitalisation for hyperkalaemia rose after publication of RALES as prescribing increased [18].

Pregnancy. Rat studies report feminisation of male fetuses, and the label advises that it may affect sex differentiation; limited human case reports have not shown an association with major malformations [3]. The NHS says it is not usually recommended in pregnancy [24].

Spironolactone and its active metabolites competitively bind aldosterone receptors in the distal nephron, increasing sodium and water excretion while retaining potassium [3]. Its antiandrogen action comes from weak antagonism of androgen receptors and reduced androgen production, which is the rationale for sebum and acne effects [1][2]. The 2012 review adds that it reduces sebaceous gland size and sebum output, raises sex hormone-binding globulin and competes with androgens at skin androgen receptors [14]. Wikipedia notes it is only a weak diuretic on its own, that oral bioavailability is about 60 to 90 percent and that the parent drug's half-life is about 1.4 hours, with longer-lasting active metabolites [1].

Wikipedia reports that progesterone's natriuretic effects were shown in 1955 and that spironolactone was developed shortly afterwards as a synthetic antimineralocorticoid analogue of progesterone. It was first synthesised in 1957, patented between 1958 and 1961 and first marketed in 1959. Gynecomastia was first reported with it in 1962, its antiandrogenic activity was first described in 1969, it was first studied for hirsutism in women in 1978 and for antiandrogen use in transgender women in 1986. Early tablets absorbed poorly, and a micronised formulation was later adopted [1]. Grokipedia attributes its development to G.D. Searle and a first US approval in 1960, though that page gives two different approval dates, so the exact date is unsettled in that source [2].

RALES in 1999 established its role in severe heart failure [7]. Off-label acne use dates from around the 1980s, according to reviews, and dermatology trials in women followed, culminating in SAFA and FASCE in 2023 and 2024 [5][6][14]. Spironolactone is on the WHO Essential Medicines List and was the 52nd most prescribed drug in the US in 2023, according to Wikipedia [1].

A study in the Journal of Drugs in Dermatology, led from George Washington University and reported by Dermatology Times in February 2025, evaluated the 50 most-viewed TikTok videos for the search '#spironolactone' (searched 11 December 2023). Thirty-nine were patient testimonials, ten educational and one a documentary; together they had more than 100 million views. The authors scored overall quality 1 of 5 on mDISCERN and 2 of 5 on the Global Quality Scale, with educational videos scoring higher, and concluded the content can mislead viewers about efficacy, stopping treatment and side effects. Senior author Dr. Adam Friedman said, 'We need guardrails on medical information disseminated via social media.' [23]

On looksmax.org it is discussed mainly as a topical antiandrogen for acne and skin texture during anabolic steroid use, and on T Nation in lists of drugs that affect hormones or breast tissue. [19][21]

Spironolactone is prescription-only in most countries and is marketed throughout the world as a generic. Aldactone is the original brand; combination products include Aldactazide, and veterinary brands also exist. The generic name is the INN, USAN and BAN; its developmental codes were SC-9420 and NSC-150339 [1].

Beyond acne and hair, Wikipedia notes spironolactone has been studied for benign prostatic hyperplasia (benefit at three months that faded by six, with gynecomastia in about 5 percent), rosacea, fibromyalgia and bulimia nervosa (not effective in the study cited), and for blocking Epstein-Barr virus production in laboratory work [1]. The AAD guideline and recent reviews of acne treatments continue to discuss its place relative to antibiotics and isotretinoin, and the SAFA authors describe it as a useful alternative to oral antibiotics for women with acne [4][5][15].

lore.intro: Spironolactone is discussed on looksmax.org mainly as a topical anti-androgen for acne and skin texture during anabolic steroid use, on T Nation in lists of drugs that affect hormones or breast tissue, and on TikTok through patient testimonials about acne. [19][21][23]

claims.claim: Topical spironolactone prevents steroid-related acne and poor skin texture without affecting hormone levels.
claims.believers: The author of a looksmax.org thread says a 2% to 5% prescription-grade cream or gel counters androgenic skin effects during a steroid cycle and, applied to the skin, does not lower testosterone [19]. A T Nation poster likewise says he had heard spironolactone cream is an effective topical anti-androgen for back acne [22].
claims.experts: A 2023 systematic review examined oral and topical spironolactone for androgen-related skin conditions [11]. No published trials have tested it in people using anabolic steroids.

claims.claim: Oral spironolactone helps hair loss caused by DHT.
claims.believers: The same looksmax.org thread says oral spironolactone can be tried for DHT-related hair loss while stating that finasteride or dutasteride is generally a better option [19].
claims.experts: A systematic review of androgenetic alopecia treatments and a review of oral and topical spironolactone describe the evidence as coming mainly from small studies [11][12].

claims.claim: Spironolactone can reduce water retention caused by growth hormone use.
claims.believers: A T Nation poster in a thread on growth hormone, quoted in the excerpt, says Aldactone helps reduce the high aldosterone and water retention that accompany HGH [20].
claims.experts: The US label describes spironolactone as an aldosterone blocker used as a diuretic in heart failure, cirrhosis and nephrotic syndrome, and Wikipedia calls it only a weak diuretic on its own [3][1]. No published studies have tested it in people using growth hormone.

claims.claim: Spironolactone can cause gynecomastia and lower androgen activity.
claims.believers: A T Nation 'Gyno Sticky' thread lists spironolactone among medications that cause 10 to 20 percent of gynecomastia cases in adults, and a quoted Wikipedia passage in another thread says it reduces testosterone production and blocks androgen receptors [21][20].
claims.experts: The US label lists gynecomastia, hyperkalemia and reduced libido among adverse effects and advises potassium monitoring [3]. Wikipedia describes weak antagonism of the androgen receptor and reduced androgen production [1].

claims.claim: Spironolactone clears hormonal acne in women.
claims.believers: Patient testimonials make up 39 of the 50 most-viewed TikTok videos on the drug, and users share their own acne experiences there. [23]
claims.experts: In the SAFA trial, women taking spironolactone had higher acne quality-of-life symptom scores than placebo at weeks 12 and 24, and the FASCE trial found greater treatment success than doxycycline at month 6; the 2024 AAD guideline makes a conditional recommendation. [4][5][6]

claims.claim: Topical spironolactone gives the benefit without systemic effects.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread says topical use does not lower testosterone [19].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports little or no systemic absorption with topical use, and a 2023 systematic review found improvement in two small topical hair-loss studies, with contact dermatitis in one; it found no head-to-head comparison with oral use. [1][11]

claims.claim: TikTok information on spironolactone can be taken at face value.
claims.believers: Viewers are drawn to testimonials, which were 78 percent of the top 50 videos. [23]
claims.experts: The George Washington University study scored the videos 1 of 5 on mDISCERN and 2 of 5 on the Global Quality Scale and concluded they can mislead about efficacy, stopping treatment and side effects. [23]

chain: Blocks androgen receptors and lowers androgen action in skin
Sebaceous glands shrink and make less oil
Fewer inflammatory acne lesions; less oily skin; slower hirsutism and thinning in women
angle.text: Dermatologists prescribe it off-label to women with persistent or hormonal-pattern acne, oily skin, unwanted hair growth and female pattern hair loss. Benefit typically builds over weeks to months, and the trials of acne show larger gains after 24 weeks than at 12 weeks. [5][14]
